meta.description: Not Galileo — Georg Cantor, in a letter of 4 November 1885 about the mathematicians who would not accept transfinite numbers.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The fear of infinity is a form of myopia that destroys the possibility of seeing the actual infinite, even though it in its highest form created and sustains us'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator credits Georg Cantor and finds no support for Galileo. The German stands on p. 7 of Cantor’s Zur Lehre vom Transfiniten (1890).

answer.label: Not Galileo — Georg Cantor, in a letter of 1885
answer.authorDates: 1845–1918 · German mathematician, founder of set theory
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator settled this in May 2025 ↗: Cantor deserves the credit, the source is a letter he wrote to the Swedish mathematician G. Eneström on 4 November 1885, and QI “has found no substantive support for the attribution to Galileo Galilei who died in 1642.” We read the German for ourselves in a printing QI does not cite — Cantor’s own Zur Lehre vom Transfiniten (Halle a. S.: C. E. M. Pfeffer, 1890), p. 7 ↗, where the piece is headed “Über die verschiedenen Standpunkte in Bezug auf das actuale Unendliche … Aus einem Schreiben des Verf. an Herrn G. Eneström in Stockholm vom 4. Nov. 1885” and the sentence runs “es läßt sich dieses Verhalten auch als eine Art Kurzsichtigkeit auffassen…” The English everyone quotes is Rudy Rucker’s, from Infinity and the Mind (1982).

source.heading: A mathematician defending his own numbers

docMeta.dd: Über die verschiedenen Standpunkte in Bezug auf das actuale Unendliche
In a letter to G. Eneström in Stockholm, 4 November 1885
Zur Lehre vom Transfiniten, Erste Abtheilung (Halle a. S.: C. E. M. Pfeffer, 1890), p. 7
Rudy Rucker, Infinity and the Mind (1982), p. 43 — per Quote Investigator

source.excerpt: … so scheint mir die damit verbundene unkritische Ablehnung des legitimen A. U. kein geringeres Vergehen wider die Natur der Dinge zu sein, die man zu nehmen hat, wie sie sind, und es läßt sich dieses Verhalten auch als eine Art Kurzsichtigkeit auffassen, welche die Möglichkeit raubt, das A. U. zu sehen, obwohl es in seinem höchsten, absoluten Träger uns geschaffen hat und erhält und in seinen secundären, transfiniten Formen uns allüberall umgiebt und sogar unserm Geiste selbst innewohnt.
trail: Quote Investigator’s article of 10 May 2025 ↗ is the anchor. It gives the earliest instance as the 1885 Eneström letter, prints the German, identifies Rucker’s 1982 Infinity and the Mind (p. 43) as the source of the English wording, and states that it has found no substantive support for the Galileo attribution.

We did not stop at the summary. Cantor collected his Zeitschrift für Philosophie und philosophische Kritik papers himself in 1890 ↗, and the first piece in that collection is the Eneström letter, headed with its date. The sentence is on p. 7 ↗ — the same German QI prints, in a printing forty-two years earlier than the one QI cites.

The letter is an argument, not an aphorism. Eneström had asked Cantor about the Abbé Moigno’s Impossibilité du nombre actuellement infini (Paris, 1884) ↗, and Cantor spends the reply dismantling the claim that actually infinite numbers are impossible — naming Cauchy, Leibniz and Gauss. The “myopia” he means is a specific refusal by named mathematicians, his contemporaries, to look at his transfinite numbers.

Why Galileo of all people gets the credit is not a mystery. Wikiquote quotes Eric Temple Bell’s The Development of Mathematics (1940) noting that Galileo observed as early as 1638 that there are precisely as many squares as positive integers ↗, and that the distinction between denumerable and non-denumerable classes was “observed about 1840 by Bolzano and in 1878 by Cantor.” The two men are next to each other in every history of the infinite. A sentence with no citation drifts to the more famous of the pair.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the Fraktur of the 1890 printing, which spells umgiebt and secundären; the 1932 collected edition modernises both, on the evidence of Quote Investigator’s transcription of it, which is the only text of that edition we could reach. “A. U.” is Cantor’s own abbreviation, used throughout the letter, for Actual-Unendliches — the actual infinite. The English in circulation also drifts by a word: Rucker’s rendering reads “even though it in its highest form has created and sustains us.”

source.rightsNote: Two different answers here. Cantor’s German is public domain — he died in 1918 and the printing we read is from 1890 ↗. The English sentence at the top of this page is not: it is Rudy Rucker’s translation, published in Infinity and the Mind (Birkhäuser, 1982) ↗, which remains in copyright. Quote it as a quotation, with the credit, and not as free text.

author.name: Georg Cantor
author.heading: About Georg Cantor
author.metaLine: 1845–1918 · German mathematician, founder of set theory
author.bio: Georg Ferdinand Ludwig Philipp Cantor was born in 1845 and spent his career at Halle, where he created set theory almost single-handedly. He established the one-to-one correspondence as the test of sameness of size, proved that the real numbers are more numerous than the natural numbers, and showed that this implies an endless hierarchy of infinities — results that a substantial part of the profession, led by Kronecker, refused to accept in his lifetime. He was a devout Lutheran who took the theological stakes of the actual infinite seriously, corresponded about them with Catholic scholars, and whose recurring bouts of depression, from 1884 to the end of his life, have been blamed on the hostility of his contemporaries. He died in 1918.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two men who thought hard about the actual infinite, 243 years apart, and only one of them wrote this sentence.

items.why: Quote Investigator states plainly that it has “found no substantive support for the attribution to Galileo Galilei who died in 1642” ↗. The sentence also appears in none of the sourced, attributed or misattributed quotations on his Wikiquote page ↗.

QI traces it to Cantor’s letter to G. Eneström ↗ and we read the German on p. 7 of Cantor’s own 1890 collection ↗, where the piece carries the letter’s date in its heading. Cantor was defending transfinite numbers against mathematicians who would not entertain them; the myopia is theirs.

QI identifies the familiar wording as Rucker’s translation, on p. 43 of his book ↗. “Myopia” for Kurzsichtigkeit and “in its highest form” for in seinem höchsten, absoluten Träger are his choices, and they are why the sentence reads like an epigram rather than a clause in a mathematical argument.

Galileo really did get there first in one respect: Wikiquote quotes E. T. Bell noting that in 1638 Galileo observed there are precisely as many squares as positive integers ↗, the property that defines an infinite set — and Bell dates Cantor’s own observation of the denumerable / non-denumerable distinction to 1878. Galileo saw the paradox. Cantor wrote the sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator credits Cantor and rules out Galileo ↗; the German is on p. 7 of Cantor’s 1890 collection ↗, under the date 4 November 1885.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Cantor was not writing about the sublime. He was losing an argument with his profession. By 1885 he had shown that infinities come in different sizes, and much of mathematical opinion — Kronecker most damagingly — treated the actual infinite as a confusion to be legislated out of existence. This sentence is what a man writes when the objection he keeps meeting is not a counter-argument but a refusal to look.

That is also why the word he chose was Kurzsichtigkeit, short-sightedness. He writes of a certain “horror infiniti” that, he says, found its classic expression and its support in a letter of Gauss’s he had mentioned earlier, and his complaint is that it is a habit of the eye rather than a result: an unwillingness to focus, not a proof of anything. The clause after the famous one ↗ says the infinite is not remote at all — that in its secondary, transfinite forms it surrounds us everywhere and is present in our own minds.
detailsBody: The letter had a specific addressee and a specific provocation. Gustaf Eneström ↗, the Swedish historian of mathematics, had written to Cantor asking whether he had read the Abbé Moigno’s pamphlet arguing that an actually infinite number is impossible and drawing theological conclusions from it. Cantor’s reply traces the position back through Cauchy to P. Gerdil (1718–1802) — whom he describes as a highly placed and respected figure and an esteemed philosopher, for a time a professor at Turin, later tutor to the future Charles Emmanuel IV of Piedmont and called to Rome by Pius VI in 1776 — disposes of it, and only then reaches the sentence people quote — which is a diagnosis of his opponents, delivered mid-argument.

The religious note in it is not decoration either. Cantor was a devout Lutheran who corresponded with Catholic theologians about the transfinite ↗, and the German says the actual infinite “in its highest, absolute bearer has created and sustains us.” Rucker’s “in its highest form” smooths that into something a poster can carry. It is a good translation of a sentence that was never meant to be quoted alone — and once it was quoted alone, it needed a famous name, and the nearest famous name in the history of infinity was Galileo.
context.pull: A. U. — Cantor’s shorthand, all through the letter, for the actual infinite.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's article of 10 May 2025 concludes that Georg Cantor deserves credit for the German version of the quotation, which appeared in a letter to G. Eneström in Stockholm dated 4 November 1885, later reprinted in the 1932 Zermelo edition of Cantor's Gesammelte Abhandlungen (start page 370, quote pages 374–375); identifies the widely used English as Rudy Rucker's in Infinity and the Mind, chapter 1, quote page 43, Birkhäuser, 1982; prints the German passage beginning "Wenn aber aus einer berechtigten Abneigung"; and states "QI has found no substantive support for the attribution to Galileo Galilei who died in 1642." Fetched via WebFetch; a direct curl from this container was refused by the site's firewall.

Page 7 of Georg Cantor's Zur Lehre vom Transfiniten, Erste Abtheilung (Halle a. S.: Verlag von C. E. M. Pfeffer / Robert Stricker, 1890) carries, in Fraktur, "und es läßt sich dieses Verhalten auch als eine Art Kurzsichtigkeit auffassen, welche die Möglichkeit raubt, das A. U. zu sehen, obwohl es in seinem höchsten, absoluten Träger uns geschaffen hat und erhält und in seinen secundären, transfiniten Formen uns allüberall umgiebt und sogar unserm Geiste selbst innewohnt." The piece is headed "Über die verschiedenen Standpunkte in Bezug auf das actuale Unendliche. Von Georg Cantor in Halle. (Aus einem Schreiben des Verf. an Herrn G. Eneström in Stockholm vom 4. Nov. 1885.)" and opens by answering Eneström's question about the Abbé Moigno's Impossibilité du nombre actuellement infini (Paris, Gauthier-Villars, 1884). Confirmed by reading the page image (page number 7) and the OCR text.

The Internet Archive holds the complete 1890 scan of Cantor's Zur Lehre vom Transfiniten: Gesammelte Abhandlungen aus der Zeitschrift für Philosophie und philosophische Kritik, Erste Abtheilung, published at Halle by C. E. M. Pfeffer (Robert Stricker), and it is not access-restricted.

Wikipedia gives Georg Cantor's dates as 3 March 1845 to 6 January 1918, and describes him as the creator of set theory, who established the importance of one-to-one correspondence, defined infinite and well-ordered sets, and proved the real numbers more numerous than the natural numbers, implying an infinity of infinities; describes him as a devout Lutheran Christian whose explicit Christian beliefs shaped his philosophy of science and who corresponded with Christian theologians about the transfinite, naming Cardinal Johann Baptist Franzelin and the neo-scholastic Konstantin Gutberlet; and records that his recurring bouts of depression from 1884 to the end of his life have been blamed on the hostile attitude of many of his contemporaries, including Kronecker's persistent criticism.
Wikipedia describes Gustaf Hjalmar Eneström (1852–1923) as a Swedish mathematician, statistician and historian of mathematics known for the Eneström index.

English Wikiquote's Galileo Galilei page does not carry "The fear of infinity is a form of myopia..." in any sourced section, nor under Attributed, nor under Misattributed. Its "Quotes about Galileo" section quotes Eric Temple Bell, The Development of Mathematics (1940), stating that Galileo observed as early as 1638 that there are precisely as many squares as positive integers, and that the distinction between denumerable and non-denumerable classes "was observed about 1840 by Bolzano and in 1878 by Cantor."

The Internet Archive holds a scan of Rudy Rucker, Infinity and the Mind: The Science and Philosophy of the Infinite (Boston: Birkhäuser, 1982), and the item is access-restricted, so its p. 43 could not be read here.
